comments.author: synapsomorphy
comments.text: Ok, so it actually flies. That was unexpected. It's an incredible engineering achievement to build in massive fans and rocket engines into a high performance car. It's truly wild. It's being sold in two modes. One with cold gas (no combustion) seemingly just for extra forwards acceleration (no flying) and one with real combustion rocket engines, the latter was in the video and is "invite only". Wild that they devoted so much effort to an economically completely infeasible model. I wonder if the combustion version will even break 3 figures sales. Even just the cold gas variant seems like a nightmare for production, there's a high pressure COPV in that thing and that's gonna make crashes much more.. exciting, and Tesla doesn't have a great record anyways. But very few of these are ever getting sold anyways.

comments.author: mNovak
comments.text: Everyone's focusing on the cold gas thrusters, which of course is very cool, but not actually shocking that it technically could be done (economically is another question). But can we talk about the just casually driving straight vertical or sticking to the ceiling? I didn't think that would be technically possible for a 1000kg+ car with probably at least 2" of ground clearance. There's presumably very limited stores of compressed gas, so you might get one hop or a couple 0-60 boosts per charge. But with electric fans, suction is a feature with much longer duration (minutes?), so you could feasibly do the batman driving on the tunnel ceiling past traffic trick.

comments.author: CommieBobDole
comments.text: So this is a really neat technical demo, using spacecraft cold-gas thrusters and guidance hardware/software to do crazy stunt stuff in a car, but what's the relevance to an actual product that can be sold, even as a small-volume exotic? These are pressurized gas thrusters, so either the tanks, valves, and piping take up most of the interior of the car, or it has a low-single-digit number of seconds of thrust before recharge, probably both. Also the tanks for these things tend to use incredibly high pressures and are apt to explode spectacularly in any sort of accident. This is sort of like demonstrating a car that softens the asphalt in front of it with lasers to get a better grip; difficult, technically impressive, and zero chance that it will ever be allowed on a public road. Edit: According to this Motor Trend article, it uses a big carbon-fiber pressure vessel at 5500psi, so basically an enormous fragile bomb. And the one that did all the stunts had two of the pressure vessels which would have filled most of the interior. https://www.motortrend.com/news/tesla-roadster-thrust-system...

comments.text: This is one of the coolest marketing stunts/demos that I have ever seen. In fact, it's the second coolest that I have ever seen, after SpaceX/Tesla's Starman. stories.title_en: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
stories.title_ja: Claude が ECDSA 曲線の起源を明らかに

comments.author: fidotron
comments.text: While this confirms the method of production it doesn't say anything about their selection, especially since they were, apparently, generated over a period of months. Specifically you cannot see those candidates that were generated and discarded. "It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator." Yes. "However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated." Does not logically follow when "doing and saying nothing" will completely suffice.

comments.author: JumpCrisscross
comments.text: “In under half an hour, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!” Gorgeous. I wonder if the NSA employee who did this suffered a head injury or has been quietly giggling to themselves for the last quarter century.

comments.author: teddyh
comments.text: > The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. The simplest explanation would be that it was generated the same way as the others, but somebody mistyped a digit somewhere along the way to publishing, and therefore a solution could not be found with the assumption that the number is correct.

comments.author: sweis
comments.text: 13 years of tinfoil hats for srand48(time(NULL)

comments.author: tptacek
comments.text: This is devastating news... for an entire generation of NIST cryptography conspiracy theories.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、ClaudeがNISTの楕円曲線（P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, P-521）のシードが、Cライブラリのlrand48（srand48）にUnixタイムスタンプをシードしただけの乱数生成結果であることを突き止めたことだ。これにより、これらの曲線がハッシュ関数などの複雑なプロセスから導出されたという長年の陰謀説が崩れ、単なるタイムスタンプベースのランダム値である可能性が示された。

賛否両論としては、シードがタイムスタンプだけで生成されたことを「無害かつ偶然」だと肯定的に受け止める意見と、タイムスタンプを公開したことが意図的な透明性の証拠になり得るという疑問、あるいは逆に「何も言わずに済ませた」だけで十分だとする批判がある。さらに、B-163シードが説明できず、タイプミスの可能性が指摘されている点も議論の焦点になった。

注目コメントでは、「たった30分でClaudeが謎を解いたのは素晴らしい」と称賛しつつ、NSA職員がこれを長年黙って楽しんでいたかもしれないという皮肉な発言が特に洞察に富んでおり、技術的発見と人間的側面を結びつけた点が挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: Claude が楕円曲線ディフィー・ヘルマン（ECDSA）の曲線パラメータがなぜ特定の値に選ばれたかを歴史的文書から解明し、暗号実装の信頼性議論に新たな視点を提供している。

comments.author: amluto
comments.text: Sadly the PR gets a detail wrong: > Implementations are expected to optimize the code generated to be as minimal as possible for the platform. For example, on X86 it’s expected that this produces a single INT3 instruction. The goal in this expectation is to place the debugger as close as possible in the caller of breakpoint() to improve the debugging experience for users. This is the wrong design on x86 at least with many debuggers. x86’s int3 is a trap and reports the address of the next instruction in the saved register state [0]. Most debuggers are not very clever and just use the saved address to generate the offending line of code and the call stack. But if the trap sequence is just int3, then the saved address could be outside the offending basic block or even outside the function entirely. gdb is certainly in the class of debuggers that get this wrong. The easy workaround is to generate int3; nop for the breakpoint instead of just int3. The saved address will point to the nop and the debugger will be happy. [0] FRED also reports the instruction length, allowing one to deduce the trapping address.

comments.author: yhjc2692
comments.text: > libjxl's maximum effort is very slow. It produces files 2–7% smaller than its default for photos, and ~25% smaller for the screenshot and illustration, but takes 9–46 seconds, which is 50–180x as long as its default. jixel gets the same results in a couple of seconds. libjxl's slow speed at efforts >7 is primarily due to an iterative evaluation-optimization loop of a perceptual error metric called Butteraugli (by tuning quantization weights). This, as well as some other computations in libjxl encoding, happen to be data-parallel and run faster on GPUs than multicore CPUs. In case anyone is interested, I've been working on a GPU-accelerated libjxl port (supporting CUDA and Metal for now) that makes this much faster, closer to libjxl's normal speeds: https://github.com/yunho-c/gjxl - geared for encoding a large batch images into JPEG XL. It's also faster by around 2.9x at normal effort (7).

I also remember the big claims about WebP's superiority, which ended-up in practice, at equivalent file-size, mostly trading away some of the JPEG artifacts that we all know for some unusual new ones. comments.author: gopalv
comments.text: > A switch statement with many cases can be compiled as a jump table (fast, O(1), but requires a full table load and indirect jump) or as a cascade of compares (slower per-case but better branch prediction if one case dominates). Switch case is the workhorse of a lexer, parser and execution engine. Lots of them over enums. This was all mis-optimized for years thanks to Spectre/Meltdown changing how the actual runtime of pre-fetch and speculation used to work. All my work on CGOTO was made irrelevant by the CPU advances, only to become relevant again when fetch speculation got nerfed. The indirect call scenario is a bit more interesting, because the JVM has an amazing paper about interface dispatch caches [1] on how to do it runtime instead of compile time. The PGO is still useful, but not unless you can predict the workload you're going to have - Benchmarketing with a TPC benchmark is a good situation for it. If you have consistent hardware, tuning an OLTP system for the hardware is much more interesting. Going back in the memory hole, Yahoo used to have a Jeremy Cole build of Mysql which was specially optimized for the raid disk layout that was in production (ZFS came by to fix those issues directly). [1] - https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/504311.504291

comments.author: shaggie76
comments.text: We've tried PGO with the Evolution engine every major Visual Studio release for as long as I can remember and each time we fail to measure a significant performance increase -- certainly not anything worth the substantial time and effort required to do it regularly. Our most recent test of LTCG was actually interesting because it seemed to move the needle enough to measure (but not enough to suffer). It appeared as though it optimized the vast majority of the code for size (inlining sparingly) and we speculate that the improvements to cache usage were the reason we saw improvements.

stories.title_en: What on Earth Is Dekton?
stories.title_ja: デクトンとは何者か？

comments.author: zebrafruit
comments.text: It’s interesting that the focus is on porcelain as a cooking surface but misses the biggest reasons for it displacing engineered quartz or granite for countertops. There’s a few factors at play here leading to the prominence of porcelain. For the induction cooktops, you can cut porcelain slabs to 6mm compared to your 3cm (sometimes 2cm) quartz and granite. This is also why you can use it for walls and floors. The thinner materials allow the magnets to actually function. The manufacturing process for engineered quartz is now being interwoven with silicosis through the legal system, leading to manufacturers marketing “low silica” quartz at a cost premium. This premium is closing the cost gap with porcelain. This is the main economic and legal reason as jurisdictions- Australia and maybe soon California look to ban these products forcing the market towards natural stones. If you’re then selecting from natural stones, porcelain is essentially used as printer paper for whatever stone pattern is desired, and given that people tend to want things that look like marble, this “ink” is essentially free for the manufacturing process, making the porcelain look like marble more than quartz or granite. Engineered quartz is also not a great exterior material, again yielding to porcelain.

comments.author: icodestuff
comments.text: I wanted Dekton for my new countertops. Its list of resistances to various kitchen mishaps was extremely impressive. Every other material we looked at has at least one weakness. Dekton was marketed as having none. It also looked quite good, being available in lots of colors and patterns. The real drawback was going to be the price. It's basically the most expensive countertop material (or was, 2 years ago). And then a ~3x3" sample I was looking at Home Depot slipped and fell on the floor, from under 3 feet in height. It landed more or less flat on its face and absolutely exploded over ~25 square feet. The internal stresses in this stuff are nuts. Then I found YouTube videos evaluating it. Everything they claim seems to be accurate, except for shatter resistance. Any sort of focused stress (one video dropped a bearing ball from a couple feet up) will absolutely wreck it. Ended up going with a high-quality quartz instead. Not as much heat resistance as Dekton, but it won't break if something falls out of a cabinet.

comments.author: throwaway219450
comments.text: The article misses an important bit of context (imo) that low thermal expansion glasses like CERAN have been around for ages and anyone who’s used an induction or a glass top stove would be familiar. However you can now get completely hidden stoves that look like stone countertops. If you’re not in the market for a kitchen, or know anyone people who recently remodeled it’s reasonable to not know they exist. I don’t know anyone with one, and everyone in our town still has gas. The author doesn’t explain which one they were buying, but it seems like the latter? Normal induction glass top stoves are a unit that drops into the countertop so of course you get the glass included (because at the very least, it has the decal for the cook zones and controller built in). The invisible ones only come with the burners so you can custom fit the top. Looks like you can get them off AliExpress even. It seems like this is the point of confusion - the author thought he could go down to a glazing shop to buy some tough glass..? I suggest go and watch Huygens Optics series about CERAN: https://youtu.be/qi8jmEbWsxU

stories.title_en: I Love Software Rendering

comments.author: buffportion
comments.text: Besides differences in texture mapping, the way GPUs render triangles is quite different to techniques commonly used in the old days. No one was computing barycentric coordinates and checking if every pixel was inside a triangle - it’s too slow to do that on a single thread. At low resolutions you get very different visual results because a GPU will not render triangles that do not cover the center of a pixel without anti-aliasing.

comments.author: delta_p_delta_x
comments.text: This isn't software rendering, it's called turning off spatial anti-aliasing. You can still do that in the modernest of modern games. Software rendering went out of the window because the CPU tends to have other things to do whilst playing the game besides only multiplying 4x4 matrices, which was shifted to the shader cores of GPUs. The look-and-feel that the author is discussing including shadow and texture LUTs can also be done on GPUs by passing the tables in to shaders as constant read-only storage buffers; that is not specific to software rendering. It bears mentioning that many modern software renderers (LLVMpipe/Lavapipe, OpenSWR, WARP) are basically full D3D/OpenGL/Vulkan devices in their own right, including shader compilers. Also, modern spatial anti-aliasing works by multisampling within a pixel (or even neighbouring pixels) and taking the average, rather than filtering across singly-sampled pixels, which massively reduces the quality. Not to mention temporal and machine learning AA techniques including DLSS, XeSS, FSR, and all the TAA implementations in many games.

comments.author: bob1029
comments.text: Software rendering often provided better visual effects than the GPU paths could provide at the time. A general purpose CPU can technically do any effect since the software is the pixel shader. Programmable shader pipelines weren't a thing until Geforce 3 in 2001.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点: ソフトウェアレンダリングとGPUの三角形 rasterization の違い、バリセントリック座標や低解像度での見た目の違い、アンチエイリアスの扱い。  
賛否両論: ソフトウェアレンダリングは当時GPUでは不可能だった独自のエフェクトを提供できたという賛意と、これは単に空間AAをオフにしただけで、現代GPUでも同等のことが可能であり、CPUには他の処理があるため実用的でないという否定的意見がある。  
注目コメント: 「サウンドカードを追加すると10fps上がった」という具体的な体験談と、LLVMpipe/Lavapipeなどの現代のソフトウェアレンダラはフル機能のGPUドライバと同等であり、シェーダーコンパイラも含むという洞察に富んだコメント。

stories.title_en: What was a Token Ring network?

comments.author: blakesterz
comments.text: The "WAS" in that title just made me feel really old. I remember learning about this in college and it being a thing that I would need to work with and understand how it works why it's different than ethernet. And now it's just a big "WAS".

comments.author: js2
comments.text: TokenRing was already an academic curiosity when I was getting my CS degree in the mid-90s. The CS department by that point had already switched to twisted-pair Ethernet. By the time of my first job in the late 90s, we used FDDI for our web farm's backend network, but we tore that out with the arrival of gigabit, so FDDI didn't last too long either.

comments.author: jwr
comments.text: We used to love token ring style networks (specifically ARCNET) for playing Doom, Descent and Quake back in the day. ARCNET was more annoying to set up and had thicker cables, but it was rock-solid reliable afterwards. Totally bulletproof. In comparison to that, traditional ethernet (think concentric cabling and terminators) glitched often and one flaky part of a cable could ruin your day. ARCNET was much slower in theory, but robust, fair and stable and did not totally die under load from a single client.

comments.author: EvanAnderson
comments.text: My local hospital system (Premier Health) was all-in on IBM and token ring. I remember being chagrined when they built a new hospital in 1998 and wired everything for token ring. The writing was clearly on the wall for token ring by 1998 but their IT department bled IBM blue. Fast-forward to 2013, when my wife was giving birth to our daughter in one of their hospitals, and I noticed an unused type-1 token ring wall jack in our room right beside some occupied 8P8C (aka RJ-45) jacks.

comments.author: alexpotato
comments.text: Fun fact: When I was an intern at Merck in the late 1990s, the networking team was switching over from Token Ring to Ethernet. It was so much work that they were openly recruiting anyone who was an employee or intern to come in on a weekend and help out. They eventually offered to pay people extra and a couple of my intern buddies took up the offer.

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
- Token Ring（およびARCNET）がかつてどのように使われていたか、特に大学・病院・ゲーム環境での実体験。  
- Ethernet・FDDI・ギガビットイーサネットへの移行過程と、その移行がもたらした作業負荷やコスト。  
- Token Ringの信頼性・公平性と、従来のイーサネットの脆弱さ（ケーブルの断線・終端不良）の比較。

**賛否両論**  
- 賛成側：ARCNET/Token Ringは設定は面倒だが、一度設置すれば極めて安定・故障に強く、ゲームや病院ネットワークで「弾丸のように」信頼できた。  
- 反対/中立側：理論上は遅く、ケーブルが太く高価で、最終的に Ethernet／ギガビットに置き換えられただけの遺産であり、移行作業は大きかった。

**注目コメント**  
- 「ARCNETはゲーム（Doom, Descent, Quake）で使われ、設定は厄介だが一度動作すれば完全に弾丸のように安定していた」という指摘。実際の負荷でも単一クライアントでネットワークが死ぬことがなく、公平かつ安定していた点が特に洞察に富んでいた。  
- また、 Merck でのインターン経験から、Token Ring から Ethernet への移行が週末ボランティア作業となり、最終的に報酬を出してでも人手を求めたというエピソードが、移行の実際の苦労を如実に示している。
stories.editor_note: トークンリングネットワークの歴史と仕組みが振り返られ、日本のレガシー産業ネットワークの近代化議論に参照点となっている。
